docs.h: How a date becomes a Pattern Day
docs.b: How a date becomes a Pattern Day The Pattern Calendar counts a year of thirteen moons, twenty-eight days each: 13 × 28 = 364 days. Those are the Pattern Days, numbered 1 to 364. One more day stands outside the count — the Day Out of Time , which belongs to no moon and no week — and in the fuller reckoning a second outside day, the Deep Time Day , stands with it. A leap arrangement keeps the count true against the civil year. To turn a civil date into its Pattern Day, the calendar counts from a fixed anchor — April 17, 2026 is Moon 1, Day 1, Pattern Day 1 — and the count is pinned by fixtures: agreed dates (July 17, 2026 = Pattern Day 92; September 15, 2026 = Pattern Day 152) that every implementation, site and app alike, must reproduce, tested against a shared set of dates both must pass. If a copy of the calendar ever disagrees with a fixture, the copy is wrong, and the fixture is how we know.
docs.p: How a date becomes a Pattern Day

docs.b: How the sky is computed The sky is worked out on your own device, at the moment you look — nothing is fetched, so nothing can be out of date, and the same sky stands in the app, which has no internet by design. Sunrise and sunset come from the sun's hour angle for your kept place; the moon's phase and lit fraction from its position against the sun; the seasons' turns are found by watching the sun's longitude cross the turn, for any year you stand in. The planets use published low-precision elements — good enough to place them honestly, and labelled with their class. The stars are a fixed catalogue of 510 bright stars, placed by the turning of the Earth (sidereal time) over your place. What "approximate" means here. Some things on the Sphere are exact counts and some are computations, and the difference is printed, not hidden. The older moon model still standing in parts of the site labels itself, in its own code, an approximate synodic phase : it counts the moon's age from a known new moon (January 6, 2000) by the average length of a moon's cycle, 29.530588853 days. That is honest arithmetic and it can be a little off the sky's exact moment — which is why, wherever it speaks, it says approximately . The newer sky engine computes the phase from the moon's actual position and is checked against published tables to within minutes. A label that says approximate is not a weakness in the instrument; it is the instrument telling you which kind of knowing you are looking at.

docs.h: The day-line: the same day, in other years
docs.b: The day-line: the same day, in other years Every year of the Pattern Calendar shares the same day positions, so one Pattern Day is the same point in every year. Pick a day, and a line runs from it to the same day last year, and five, ten, twenty, thirty years back — and one year forward. What the line may honestly show depends on the kind of thing: Computed things — the sky, the feasts of the computed calendars — truly run forward, because the mathematics holds next year as surely as last. Recorded things — weather, salmon, your own kept days — stop at today. The forward bead stands open and labelled: no record; the year is not kept yet. Next year's weather drawn on the line would be made up, and this instrument does not make things up. Gaps stay gaps. A year with no record shows an open bead, named as no record — never a nearby value stretched onto the day. On the pattern graph, threads join a kind of thing across the years: a straight thread is a true rhythm, a leaning thread is drift, a broken thread is a year it did not happen. Threads are labelled honestly — same kind, not the same thing — and a thread claims a real link only where a record's own rhythm links them.
docs.p: The day-line: the same day, in other years

docs.h: The labels — how this site grades what it says
docs.b: The labels — how this site grades what it says Everything the Codex states carries a grade, and the grade is part of the statement. These are the labels, explained once, here, as the site's single reference: Verified record A document, dataset, or artefact that can be opened and checked — a published table, a signed order, a counted record. The strongest grade: do not take our word; take the record's. Firsthand observation Seen or measured directly by the one reporting it — a day witnessed, a value read off the instrument. Strong, and bounded by the observer. Reported statement What someone said, carried as what they said — attributed, not endorsed. A report being repeated is not a report being confirmed. Allegation A claim made against a party or about an event, not yet established. It stands labelled as an allegation until a record settles it, one way or the other. Inference A conclusion drawn from the above — reasoning, shown as reasoning. An inference may be sound and still be wrong; it never borrows the grade of what it was drawn from. Unresolved claim A claim the record does not yet settle. It stays open, in the open, until evidence closes it. The story has its own, separate labelling, and the two never trade clothes: an episode is labelled a story on its face, the tale and the account are kept in different books, and nothing in the story is ever cited as evidence.
docs.p: The labels — how this site grades what it says

docs.b: The two senses, and their permissions The app asks for two permissions, each only when you choose to open that sense, and each refused just as easily: Calendar (READ_CALENDAR): if you grant it, the app reads your calendar events on the device so it can set them beside your days on the Pattern calendar. Events are read and shown on the device only. Photos (READ_MEDIA_IMAGES; READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE on older Android): if you grant it, the app reads your photos' dates and small thumbnails on the device so it can set your pictures by day and propose groupings. It does not copy, upload, or alter your photos. Deny either permission and the app works without that sense. You can revoke either at any time in Android's settings.

docs.b: Evidence and Research · Sources Where Every Number Comes From The Sphere shows numbers — fish counted at a dam, blossoms recorded in Kyoto, the sun worked out for your own place. This page is the receipt shelf: for each set of numbers, what it is, who publishes it, what years it covers, when we read it, and what is honestly missing. If a number on the Sphere cannot be traced to a line on this page, it does not belong on the Sphere. Plain words first. The publishers' own names for their data stand in each card, one step down, for anyone who wants to check at the source. How to read a card Counted — somebody stood there and counted, year after year.

The number is a record. Computed — worked out by mathematics on your own device, from the real motions of the sun, moon, and planets. Nothing is fetched and nothing can go stale. Kept — Aaron's own record: his study years and kept days. It is labelled as his wherever it stands, and never mixed with the counted or computed sets. The gaps are part of the record. Where a source has missing years, this page says so, and the Sphere draws the gap as a gap. How the Sphere itself works — the calendar, the sky, and the labels it uses — is on the Methods page . Salmon at Bonneville — counted Every autumn and spring, fish swim up the Columbia River past Bonneville Dam, and they are counted, one by one, day by day.
Check the workings How the Sphere knows — Methods → Open the Sphere →

The Sphere's salmon layer draws those counts: pick a day, and the same day in other years answers with the count that was recorded on it. What it is Daily counts of adult salmon and steelhead passing Bonneville Dam on the Columbia River, for four runs: Chinook, steelhead, sockeye, and coho. Young fish (jacks) are not included, and the wild-steelhead column is a part of the steelhead count, not an extra count. Who counts and publishes The counts are made by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers at the dam and published by Columbia River DART (Columbia Basin Research, University of Washington) as its Adult Passage Daily Counts. Years covered 1939–2026. Counted days held: Chinook 23,303 · steelhead 25,769 · sockeye 9,232 · coho 5,815 (coho from 1980 — see the gaps). When we read it November 23, 2026 — one file per calendar year, taken from DART's own tables. Re-reading the source is a deliberate act; the copy on the Sphere carries its read date. Checked against A day any reader can look up: September 1, 2023 reads Chinook 41,510 and steelhead 3,092 in DART's published table, and the same in the Sphere's copy. The honest gaps. DART labels Bonneville “[1938]” — the dam's first counting year — but serves no daily counts for 1938, so the record here begins in 1939 and says so. Coho were not counted separately before 1980: the coho column is empty for every day of 1939–1979, so the Sphere holds coho from 1980 and draws the earlier years as gaps.

A few published counts are negative (a correction the counters themselves printed); they are kept as published, not tidied away. Kyoto cherry blossoms — counted, across twelve centuries For over a thousand years, people in Kyoto wrote down the day the cherry trees reached full bloom — in court diaries, temple chronicles, and modern records. It is the longest single thread the Sphere can hold: one city, one tree, one day a year. What it is The date of full flowering of the cherry blossoms in Kyoto, Japan, one date per year. Who keeps it The record was gathered by Yasuyuki Aono (Osaka Prefecture University) from historical documents and modern observation.

docs.h: Kyoto cherry blossoms — counted, across twelve centuries
docs.b: The Sphere's copy reads his own workbook for the years to 2015, and Our World in Data's continuation of the same record (published under CC BY 4.0) for 2016–2026. Years covered 812–2026 — 838 years carry a recorded date. The earliest full bloom in the record is March 25, 2023; the latest, May 4, 1323. When we read it November 23, 2026. The university's own page did not answer, so Aono's workbook was read from the Internet Archive's saved copy of his page; his name stands in the file's own record of who made it. The honest gaps. Of the 1,215 years from 812 to 2026, 377 have no surviving record — no document, no date. On the Sphere the thread breaks where the record breaks; a missing year is drawn as a missing year. One correction, made openly: for 1923, Aono's workbook gives the year's 97th day (April 7) while Our World in Data's current table gives the 98th. Two independent copies of the record agree with Aono, so the Sphere carries 97 — the compiler's own hand outranks a copyist's slip — and the disagreement is written down here rather than smoothed over.
docs.p: Kyoto cherry blossoms — counted, across twelve centuries

docs.h: The sky — computed on your device
docs.b: The sky — computed on your device The sunrises, moon phases, and stars on the Sphere are not downloaded. They are worked out, on the device in your hand, from the real motions of the sun, moon, planets, and stars — so the same sky stands on the website and inside the app, which by design has no internet connection at all. What it is Sunrise, sunset, solar noon, and the length of daylight; the moon's phase and how much of it is lit; when the moon rises and sets; the dates the seasons turn, for any year; where the planets stand; and 510 bright stars placed over your place. Computed from Standard published astronomy, running entirely on the device: the sun's times by the hour-angle method used in the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's solar calculations; the planets from Paul Schlyter's published low-precision elements (their accuracy class is named in the code, not hidden); the stars from the Astronomical Almanac Bright Star List (epoch 2016.5, drawn from the Yale Bright Star Catalogue), keeping every star of magnitude 4.00 or brighter. Checked against Published tables read November 23, 2026: Seattle sun and moon tables (sunrise and sunset within 3 minutes; moonrise and moonset within 10; the moon's lit fraction within 1.5 points), the U.S. Naval Observatory's season table (within 20 minutes), and the equinox table below (within 30 minutes).
docs.p: The sky — computed on your device

docs.h: The sky — computed on your device
docs.b: Three stars whose minus signs were dropped in copying the star list — Sirius, Canopus, and Arcturus — were restored and the correction documented. The season turns For 2026 and 2027 the face has long printed the U.S. Naval Observatory's published instants (read November 20, 2026). The sky engine now finds the turns itself for any year, by watching the sun's longitude cross the turn — and where the Observatory's table stands, the table keeps precedence. The equinox table Under the calendar's study years stands a table of March equinox instants for 2014–2027 , copied into the site from a published table (janmr.com) and checked against a second, independent table: the two agree to within about 2 seconds, inside the table's stated 3-second tolerance. Stated plainly: the chain back to the original computation is only partly documented in the site's files, and the file itself says so. It is used as a check, not as an authority. What the sky does not do. No place kept, no sun times — the Sphere will not guess where you are. Below the horizon, nothing is drawn standing up. And the weather strip (temperature, air, and kin) is a different thing from the computed sky: it is fetched from the Open-Meteo services when a place is kept and the network answers, and when it cannot arrive, the face prints one honest sentence instead of a number.
docs.p: The sky — computed on your device

docs.h: The farm record — 39 counties of Western Washington
docs.b: The farm record — 39 counties of Western Washington The garden's planting windows — when a crop can go in the ground, county by county — were built from published climate records and extension teaching, not from habit. Every window in the underlying data carries the source it came from. What it is Planting windows and frost dates for all 39 Washington counties , entered November 20, 2026. Spring windows are counted in weeks from each county's average last spring frost, the way almanac and extension calendars count them. Who publishes the ground truth Each county is anchored on a named station in the NOAA U.S. Climate Normals 1991–2020 (the thirty-year climate record published by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) — its published frost dates and frost-free season length. Planting teaching comes from Washington State University Extension (the Snohomish, Skagit, and King County charts and tip sheets, including the fall and winter garden chart and the tomato rule: transplant around mid-May, once the soil is at 50°F or warmer), the Farmer's Almanac seed-starting and frost tables (which count a 30% chance of frost after the date, where NOAA's median counts the middle year — where the two disagree, both answers are kept and the disagreement written into the crop's notes), and the 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map . The one computed county One county has no NOAA normals station of its own.
docs.p: The farm record — 39 counties of Western Washington

docs.h: The farm record — 39 counties of Western Washington
docs.b: Its dates are computed from named neighbouring anchors by a stated rule, and its entry says it is computed and names its anchors. Where a county's safe planting line was not itself published, it follows the garden's stated safe rule — ten days after the median last frost — and is labelled a rule, not a measurement. The teaching shelf Beside the windows stands a teaching set of 42 sourced guides for the garden. A crop or window with no sourced value is left out of the record entirely — never guessed. The calendar's fixtures — and the study years The calendar itself is arithmetic, and arithmetic can be checked.

docs.h: The calendar's fixtures — and the study years
docs.b: The calendar is pinned by fixtures — agreed dates that every copy of the calendar, on the site and in the app, must reproduce exactly, tested by a shared set of test dates both must pass: April 17, 2026 = Moon 1, Day 1, Pattern Day 1. July 17, 2026 = Moon 4, Day 8, Pattern Day 92. September 15, 2026 = Moon 6, Day 12, Pattern Day 152. November 23, 2026 = Moon 8, Day 25, Pattern Day 221. Beside the kept record stands the alignment ledger : Aaron's own study dataset covering the civil years 2014–2027 . Those are study years — years examined, not years any keeper lived inside this calendar — and they stand on the Sphere labelled as study years, carrying only what is truly documented there. A fuller census of long records examined for the Sphere — sunspots back to 1749, river flow, ice dates six centuries long, and more, including the ones that failed the test and why — is kept with the Sphere's build records. This page lists what the Sphere actually shows. Where to Next

docs.b: Living Time · A guided practice Read Your Own Day Every day in the Codex has an address: a Moon, a day of the Moon, and a Pattern Day in the year. This short practice teaches you to read yours — not by reading about it, but by doing it, with the Spark leading and your own hands on the steps. Four small steps, a few minutes: find today, see it on the Sphere, learn what a day holds, and witness this one. Nothing here is a test, and nothing is kept against you for days away. Today loads with your local time. The practice The Spark Walk with me. In four small steps you will find today, see it on the Sphere, learn what a day holds, and witness this one — with your own hands.

The steps appear here, one at a time. If the guided road cannot run on this device, the doors below still take you everywhere it goes: the Sphere shows today lit among the year's days, and Day Notes on the 13 Moons page is where a day is witnessed with a line of your own. Open the Sphere → Open Day Notes → Find today See it on the Sphere What a day holds Witness today The rules — all of them What this practice keeps Only your place. The practice remembers which step you reached, in this browser, on this device — so the Spark can keep your place and welcome you back to it. That is all it stores.

Your day's record is made on the day itself. This page writes no record for you. When you add a line in Day Notes, that note is a real record in your own Life Atlas — yours, on your device. One calendar, read live. Every number here comes from the same Pattern Calendar the Sphere and the 13 Moons page read, computed from your own local day at the moment you look. No second clock, no stored dates. Nothing is kept against you. No pace to hold, no count of missed days. Come back when you come back; the road keeps your place. A short spoken tour of the Scripture edition's sources page: its three completeness levels, the pinned sources behind the Hebrew, the lexicon, and the English, and the limits the edition declares about itself. Press play and let the page explain itself. Your browser does not support the video element. The same tour is written out across this page. Three completeness levels Level Status Detail 1. Original word and morphology imported 37325 words and 57818 word parts imported from OSHB and machine-compared to the pinned source files by the validation suite; no independent scholarly collation is claimed. 2. Lexical senses imported-from-dataset 2460 of 2460 lemmas have BDB entries in the OSHB dataset (7251 sense records); 0 show an unavailable state. The OSHB BDB file is a work-in-progress digitisation, so senses are limited to what it contains. 3. Reviewed contextual interpretation not-started-for-review 54 draft selections; 0 reviewed. No chapter is labelled linguistically verified. Sources Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC), lemma and morphology: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible, commit dated 2024-08-27 ( pinned source edition ; exact commit 3d15126fb1ef74867fc1434be1942e837932691f ). Attribution: “Original work of the Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible available at https://github.com/openscriptures/morphhb”. WLC text is public domain; OSHB data layer is CC BY 4.0 . Morphology code legend: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible, parsing/HebrewMorphologyCodes.html at that pinned commit. The displayed parses mechanically decode OSHB codes; unrecognized codes remain explicitly marked. Lexicon: Brown–Driver–Briggs (1906, public domain) and Strong’s, with OSHB mapping/digitisation from HebrewLexicon at the commit dated 2019-09-02 ( pinned source edition ; exact commit 21c9add13bc727d3a951361778e97e3ff7afd1ce ). Each BDB panel gives the lexicon citation and dataset record ID. English: World English Bible, published by eBible.org and public domain per the included notice. The pinned copy is from TehShrike/world-english-bible , commit dated 2025-11-24 (exact commit 68669ba3be9719ae4d1135b19d9e0b6587b7c356 ). Its copyright notice says the files were generated 2017-06-14 from source files dated 2017-06-14. eBible.org was unreachable during acquisition; this copy has not been independently compared with the publisher’s edition, so publisher-edition fidelity remains unverified. File checksums are in sources/r2-02/SOURCES.json ; reports are in site-audit/r2-02/ . Limits Versification: Hebrew (WLC) numbering is used; where English Bibles number differently (e.g. Gen 32, Exod 8) the verse shows the English reference. No MT other than WLC, no Septuagint, Dead Sea Scrolls or Samaritan text is loaded. The reader does not assert variants from those witnesses; tradition notes citing them are marked “needs-source-check”. Transliteration is mechanical and approximate (it does not distinguish every shewa or qamets). Ancient pronunciation is reconstructed and debated. Consonantal display hides vowel and cantillation marks visually; the underlying text is unchanged. No Paleo-Hebrew view is offered. The word-by-word tables list every word part with its OSHB lemma and morphology code. Occurrence lists are references only; the Hebrew of other books is not loaded here. Privacy Your place, display preferences and bookmarks are stored in this browser’s localStorage only and are never transmitted. Where to Next Genesis & Exodus Scripture →

docs.b: Exodus 3 Hebrew: WLC (OSHB) · English: World English Bible · 22 verses (Hebrew numbering) Context: The burning bush and the divine name (draft, unreviewed) Literary observations The name-revelation (3:13-15) turns on the verb hayah ('to be'); 'ehyeh' is first person singular imperfect. Background 'ehyeh asher ehyeh' (3:14) is translated in several ways ('I am who I am', 'I will be what I will be', 'I will be who I will be'), because the imperfect can express present or future. Where interpreters differ How should 'ehyeh asher ehyeh' be translated? I AM WHO I AM (common English rendering) I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE (common alternative; reflects the imperfect) 1 וּמֹשֶׁ֗ה הָיָ֥ה רֹעֶ֛ה אֶת־ צֹ֛אן יִתְר֥וֹ חֹתְנ֖וֹ כֹּהֵ֣ן מִדְיָ֑ן וַיִּנְהַ֤ג אֶת־ הַצֹּאן֙ אַחַ֣ר הַמִּדְבָּ֔ר וַיָּבֹ֛א אֶל־ הַ֥ר הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים חֹרֵֽבָה׃ Now Moses was keeping the flock of Jethro, his father-in-law, the priest of Midian, and he led the flock to the back of the wilderness, and came to God’s mountain, to Horeb. docs.b: Genesis 1 Hebrew: WLC (OSHB) · English: World English Bible · 31 verses (Hebrew numbering) Context: Creation account (draft, unreviewed) Literary observations Repeated formulae structure the days: 'God said', 'and it was so', 'God saw that it was good', and the refrain 'there was evening and there was morning'. Days 1-3 and 4-6 are often read as parallel (settings and then what fills them); this is a common observation about the structure, not a claim in the text. Background The word bara ('created') is used in this chapter with God as its only subject. Where interpreters differ How is the first verse constructed? Main clause: 'In the beginning God created' (traditional reading, reflected in most English translations) Dependent construction: 'When God began to create' / 'In the beginning of God's creating' (Rashi (summary; unchecked)) 1 בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית בָּרָ֣א אֱלֹהִ֑ים אֵ֥ת הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם וְאֵ֥ת הָאָֽרֶץ׃ In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. Context notes for this verse (draft, unreviewed) Rashi (11th c.) on Gen 1:1 — Jewish medieval commentary (needs-source-check): Rashi reads bereshit as in a construct relationship ('in the beginning of God's creating') rather than as an absolute 'in the beginning'. The Hebrew allows both readings because of the vowel pointing's relation to the following verb. Edition and page not verified in this build. John 1:1-3 (New Testament) — Christian reception (needs-source-check): John 1:1 opens with 'In the beginning' and speaks of creation through the Word, widely recognised as echoing Gen 1:1-3. This is a Christian reading of the creation account, distinct from the Hebrew lexical meaning of reshit or davar. Not verified against an edition. Remnant: the Scroll’s own words beside this verse Author’s interpretation, shown unmodified from the preserved manuscript. It is not Scripture and not a lexical claim. docs.b: Genesis 2 Hebrew: WLC (OSHB) · English: World English Bible · 25 verses (Hebrew numbering) Context: The human, the garden and the first command (draft, unreviewed) Literary observations Gen 2:4 introduces the first toledot ('generations/account') formula, which recurs in Genesis as a marker of narrative sections (the formula's occurrences can be found with the lemma index). Background The ground (adamah), the human (adam) and tilling (avad) are tied together by sound and by the narrative. Where interpreters differ What does 'le-ovdah u-leshomrah' (2:15) refer to? Care of the garden (common reading) Grammatical antecedent is the feminine 'adamah' (grammatical observation (suffix is feminine; 'gan' is masculine)) 1 וַיְכֻלּ֛וּ הַשָּׁמַ֥יִם וְהָאָ֖רֶץ וְכָל־ צְבָאָֽם׃ The heavens, the earth, and all their vast array were finished. docs.b: Genesis 3 Hebrew: WLC (OSHB) · English: World English Bible · 24 verses (Hebrew numbering) Context: The nachash, the tree and the consequences (draft, unreviewed) Literary observations The wordplay arum/arumim connects chapters 2 and 3. The speakers' choice of the divine name changes in the dialogue (the serpent says 'Elohim', the narrator says 'YHWH Elohim'); this is an observable feature of the text. Background The text does not identify the serpent with any figure other than a creature of the field; later identifications are interpretive traditions. 1 וְהַנָּחָשׁ֙ הָיָ֣ה עָר֔וּם מִכֹּל֙ חַיַּ֣ת הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָׂ֖ה יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהִ֑ים וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל־ הָ֣אִשָּׁ֔ה אַ֚ף כִּֽי־ אָמַ֣ר אֱלֹהִ֔ים לֹ֣א תֹֽאכְל֔וּ מִכֹּ֖ל עֵ֥ץ הַגָּֽן׃ Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” Context notes for this verse (draft, unreviewed) H5175 (draft-unreviewed): nachash is the ordinary Hebrew word for serpent in the BDB outline. The verse itself calls it a creature of the field that YHWH God made; it does not name any other identity. Later identifications are interpretations, not lexical senses. Rashi on Gen 3:1 — Jewish medieval commentary (needs-source-check): Rashi links arum ('cunning') of the nachash with arumim ('naked') in Gen 2:25, a wordplay present in the Hebrew text itself. Not verified against an edition. Remnant: the Scroll’s own words beside this verse Author’s interpretation, shown unmodified from the preserved manuscript. It is not Scripture and not a lexical claim. docs.h: Genesis 6 — Scripture · Scroll of Fire Genesis chapter 6: Hebrew (WLC), English (WEB), word study, context and the Scroll's own commentary kept separate. Literary observations Background Where interpreters differ
docs.b: Genesis 6 Hebrew: WLC (OSHB) · English: World English Bible · 22 verses (Hebrew numbering) Context: Sons of God, daughters of men, nefilim (draft, unreviewed) Literary observations Gen 6:1-4 is a short, compressed unit; its relation to the flood narrative is debated. Background The Hebrew bene ha-elohim ('sons of God') appears in other biblical passages (e.g. Job 1:6). Where interpreters differ Who are the 'sons of God'? Divine/heavenly beings (attested in early Jewish interpretation, including the Septuagint-era tradition and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan (summary; unchecked)) Human rulers or nobles (attributed to Targum Onkelos and some medieval commentators (summary; unchecked)) Descendants of Seth (attributed to some early Christian writers (summary; unchecked)) 1 וַֽיְהִי֙ כִּֽי־ הֵחֵ֣ל הָֽאָדָ֔ם לָרֹ֖ב עַל־ פְּנֵ֣י הָֽאֲדָמָ֑ה וּבָנ֖וֹת יֻלְּד֥וּ לָהֶֽם׃ When men began to multiply on the surface of the ground, and daughters were born to them, Remnant: the Scroll’s own words beside this verse Author’s interpretation, shown unmodified from the preserved manuscript. It is not Scripture and not a lexical claim. docs.b: אָדָם — adam — Full Hebrew Treatment (Finished, Nov 23, 2026) Labels follow Aaron's rule: observation / interpretation / hypothesis / declaration are kept separate. This study belongs to a cluster — read it with אֲדָמָה ( adamah , the ground) and אֱנוֹשׁ ( enosh , the mortal). The three words answer each other, and Genesis plays them against each other on purpose. 1. The word itself Consonantal text: אדם (aleph–dalet–mem) Pointed text: אָדָם Transliteration: ʾāḏām — "ah-DAHM" Strong's / lexicon: H120; TWOT 25a Part of speech: masculine noun Frequency: BDB's entry is headed 560 — the word occurs roughly 560 times. Counts in the 550s appear in other concordances; the method (occurrences vs. verses, inclusion of the proper name) moves the number. Quote it as "about 560" and name the method. Forms: almost always singular in form. There is no true plural of אָדָם in Biblical Hebrew; where English wants "men," Hebrew uses בְּנֵי ( הָ ) אָדָם , "sons of (the) adam" — literally "children of the human" (Gen 11:5; Ps 8 passim in the singular). The construct form is the same as the absolute except in Prov 6:12. With the article, הָאָדָם , it is "the human / the man" — the generic figure of Genesis 2–3. Without the article, in later texts, it can be the proper name Adam. 2. Root — three candidates, none proven This word's etymology is genuinely unsettled, and the study must not pretend otherwise. From אָדַם ( ʾāḏam , H119), "to be red / ruddy." Strong's derives אָדָם from this verb: "ruddy, i.e. a human being." The family is real — אָדֹם ( ʾāḏōm , "red," H122), אֹדֶם ( ʾōḏem , a red gem, sardius/carnelian, H124), דָּם ( dām , "blood," H1818) all live in the same sound-neighbourhood. But "related sounds" is not a derivation. The NAS concordance pointedly gives the origin as "an unused word," i.e. it declines Strong's derivation. From אֲדָמָה ( adamah ), the ground. The biblical text's own wordplay (Gen 2:7) ties the human to the ground he was formed from. Whether that is historical etymology or the narrator's theological wordplay is debated; as the text's own claim about what a human is , it stands regardless of the etymology question. See the adamah study. A loan or shared old Semitic word. BDB lists Phoenician אדם and Sabaean (South Arabian) ʾdm with the same meaning, so the word is old and regional, not a Hebrew coinage. BDB also reports an Assyrian admu , "young (of a bird)," proposed by one scholar and disputed by another (Nöldeke) — printed here as what it is: a proposal that did not win agreement. Observation: the lexica disagree, on the record. Do not upgrade: "adam means red" and "adam means earthling" are both preachable lines; neither is a settled lexicon finding. What is settled is the usage — §3. 3. Semantic range (BDB) A human being — an individual person, male or female (Gen 2:22–25 uses it across the man/woman distinction; the word itself is not the word for "male" — that is אִישׁ , ʾîsh , or זָכָר , zākhār ). Mankind, humankind collectively — Gen 1:26–27; 5:1–2; 9:5–6. Gen 5:2 is explicit: "male and female he created them... and called their name adam." The species-name covers both sexes in the text's own words. The proper name Adam — the first man as an individual (Gen 4:25; 5:3–5; 1 Chron 1:1). Scholars debate exactly where the generic becomes the name; Genesis 2–3 mostly writes הָאָדָם , "the human," with the article — a figure, not yet a name-tag. A place name — a city in the Jordan valley (Josh 3:16, H121). Included so the concordance count is honest. 4. Biblical examples, by sense — Genesis first, where the weight is The species, made in the image — Gen 1:26–27. "Let us make adam in our image... male and female he created them." Here adam is the kind, not an individual, and the image of God is predicated of the kind, both sexes, in one breath. The groundling, formed and breathed into — Gen 2:7. docs.b: אֲדָמָה — adamah — Full Hebrew Treatment (Finished, Nov 23, 2026) Labels follow Aaron's rule: observation / interpretation / hypothesis / declaration are kept separate. This is the ground-word of the adam cluster — read it with אָדָם ( adam , the human) and אֱנוֹשׁ ( enosh , the mortal). 1. The word itself Consonantal text: אדמה (aleph–dalet–mem–he) Pointed text: אֲדָמָה Transliteration: ʾăḏāmâ — "ah-dah-MAH" Strong's / lexicon: H127 Part of speech: feminine noun Frequency: BDB's entry is headed 224; the KJV concordance count is 225. Quote as "about 225," method named — the one-occurrence difference is a counting-method artefact, and this study will not pretend to know which artefact. Forms: construct אַדְמַת ( ʾaḏmaṯ , "ground/land of —"), e.g. אַדְמַת מִצְרַיִם , "the land of Egypt" (Gen 47:20); suffixed אַדְמָתִי , "my ground" (Job 31:38); plural אֲדָמוֹת (Ps 49:12 [Eng. 49:11]) — the plural is rare, because the word usually names the one ground under your feet, not grounds in general. 2. Root — and an honest warning about direction Strong's derives adamah "from H119" ( אָדַם , "to be red"): "soil, from its general redness." BDB is visibly less sure: its entry floats the tilled-ground picture, then reports a comparison with Arabic ʾadama , "skin" — the ground as the earth's skin, smoothly covering and close-fitting — and a possible root דם with an Arabic verb "to smear, spread over a surface." The warning: even the direction of derivation inside this family is disputed. Does adam come from adamah (the human named from his ground), does adamah come from adam, or do both hang on the red-root? The lexica do not settle it, and the famous Gen 2:7 wordplay works in the text whichever way the history ran. Preachers pick a direction; this study prints the dispute. Observation: Gen 2:7 and 3:19 tie adam to adamah in the text itself. That is a textual fact, independent of etymology. Do not upgrade: "adamah means red soil" is Strong's gloss, not a consensus. Red soils exist in the land; the word's meaning in use is ground/land, full stop (§3). 3. Semantic range (BDB) Ground as tilled, yielding sustenance — the farmer's ground: Gen 2:5, 9; 4:2–3; Deut 28 passim; Prov 12:11, "he who works his adamah will have plenty of bread." A piece of ground, landed property — Gen 47:18–26, where Egypt's adamah is bought, sold, and taxed; Ps 49:12's plural, men naming "their adamot" after themselves (a shem-theme: see the shem study). Earth as material substance — what things are made of: Gen 2:7 (the human), 2:19 (the animals), Exod 20:24 (an altar of adamah), Isa 45:9 (the clay arguing with the potter). Ground as the earth's visible surface — Gen 1:25; 6:20; the face of the adamah, פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה , a fixed phrase: what the flood covers (Gen 7:23), what man is driven from (Gen 4:14). Land, territory, country — approaching אֶרֶץ ( ʾereṣ ): "the adamah of Judah" (Isa 19:17), and above all Ezekiel's אַדְמַת יִשְׂרָאֵל , "the land of Israel" (16+ times in Ezekiel) — the land as promised and given. The whole inhabited earth — rare and elevated: Gen 12:3 and 28:14, "all the families of the adamah" (see §4). The centre of gravity: adamah is worked, owned, promised earth — nearer and more handled than the cosmic אֶרֶץ . It is the ground in relation to the human who stands on it, tills it, is made of it, and is buried in it. 4. Biblical examples — the curse-and-lifting arc, Genesis first Before the human — Gen 2:5. "No shrub of the field was yet in the land, and no plant had yet sprung up... and there was no adam to work the adamah." The pair is introduced as a pair, two verses before the forming. The text wants the words heard together. The forming — Gen 2:7. Dust ( עָפָר ) of the adamah is the raw material. Note the precision: adam is not formed from adamah as a block; he is dust of it — the ground at its finest and loosest. The wordplay is adam/adamah; the material word is ʿāpār, dust. docs.b: דָּבָר — davar — Full Hebrew Treatment (Finished, Nov 23, 2026) Labels follow Aaron's rule: observation / interpretation / hypothesis / declaration are kept separate. This is the eighth study on the shelf, and the word beneath Aaron's own name for the light of it — Or HaDabar, "the Light of the Word" (§10). The text's own data is marked as such; interpretation is labelled interpretation. 1. The word itself Consonantal text: דבר (dalet–bet–resh) Pointed text: דָּבָר Transliteration: dāvār (commonly written dabar or davar ) Strong's / lexicon: H1697 Part of speech: masculine noun Occurrences: roughly 1,440 times in the Hebrew Bible — among the most frequent nouns in the whole text. 2. Root and morphology Root: ד־ב־ר ( d-b-r ). The verb dibbēr ( דִּבֵּר , Piel) means "to speak"; the noun is what is spoken — and then, by the word's own reach, the thing spoken about. Common forms: דָּבָר — davar , a word / a matter דְּבַר — devar- , "word of…" (construct: devar YHWH , "the word of YHWH") דְּבָרִים — devarim , "words" — the Hebrew name of the book of Deuteronomy is simply דְּבָרִים , "Words." דִּבְרֵי — divrei , "words of…" ( divrei hayamim , "the matters of the days" — the Hebrew title of Chronicles is literally "Words/Matters of the Days": a chronicle is a book of devarim because words and events are the same noun.) 3. Semantic range — the heart of this word Davar refuses to split what English splits. Its range: Word, speech, utterance — what is said. Command, promise, decree — what is said by one with authority. Matter, affair, business — the thing under discussion ("the matter of the king"). Thing, event, occurrence — the thing itself, out in the world. This is the word's documented centre, not a preacher's flourish: in Hebrew thought as the text itself uses it, a davar is a word with the weight of a thing. When YHWH speaks a davar , it does not describe reality from outside — it arrives as an event inside it (see §4, Isaiah 55:11). 4. Biblical examples Genesis 15:1 — "The devar of YHWH came to Abram in a vision." The word comes , like a traveller or a messenger — it has movement and presence. Deuteronomy 1:1 — "These are the devarim that Moses spoke." A whole book is a man's words, and the words are treated as events that carry a nation. Exodus 34:28 — the tablets hold aseret hadevarim , "the Ten Words" — not "commandments" in the Hebrew. The covenant's core is ten words . 1 Samuel 3:1 — " Devar YHWH was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision." A famine measured not in bread but in word. Psalm 33:6 — " Bidvar YHWH the heavens were made" — by the davar of YHWH. Creation by word, stated as mechanism, in poetry. Isaiah 55:11 — "So shall my davar be that goes out from my mouth: it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish what I purpose." The word as something sent, travelling, working, and returning with a report. 5. Wordplay the text itself plays דָּבָר / דֶּבֶר ( davar / dever , "plague") — same letters, different vowels. Exodus 9:3 sends a dever on Egypt's livestock: the dark twin of the word — a "word" of judgment that is also a thing in the world. מִדְבָּר ( midbar , "wilderness") — built on the same root letters: the place where the word is heard. Israel receives the devarim in the midbar — the word-place. Traditional teachers have leaned on this for centuries: the wilderness is where speech becomes audible because everything else is quiet. דְּבוֹרָה ( Devorah , Deborah) — the prophetess's name is "bee," from the same root field: the creature whose hum is a kind of speech, and whose sting is a word that lands as a thing. 6. Semitic cognates (where justified) Aramaic / Syriac: dabar carries "lead, guide, conduct" — the root's older undertone of arranging and directing what is spoken of. Arabic: the root d-b-r gives tadbīr — management, arrangement, directing of affairs. Across the family, the root keeps joining speech to ordering : to speak a matter is to set it in order. docs.b: אֱנוֹשׁ — enosh — Full Hebrew Treatment (Finished, Nov 23, 2026) Labels follow Aaron's rule: observation / interpretation / hypothesis / declaration are kept separate. This is the mortal-word of the adam cluster — read it with אָדָם ( adam , the species) and אֲדָמָה ( adamah , the ground). Where adam says what a human is made of and for , enosh says what a human is up against : he dies, he is frail, and he cannot cure himself. 1. The word itself Consonantal text: אנוש (aleph–nun–vav–shin) Pointed text: אֱנוֹשׁ Transliteration: ʾĕnôš — "en-OSH" Strong's / lexicon: H582; TWOT 136a. The proper name Enosh is a separate entry, H583. Part of speech: masculine noun Frequency — method matters here more than usual. The noun occurs 42 times in the Masoretic text by the usual concordance count, and it is heavily concentrated: BDB's own distribution note reads "mostly in poetry — 18 times in Job, 13 times in the Psalms," with most of the rest in Isaiah and a handful elsewhere. Some online concordances print numbers in the hundreds for this entry; those counts fold in other forms and the Aramaic cognate (Dan 7's bar enash and kin). Do not quote any count for enosh without its method; the poetry concentration, not the raw total, is the fact that matters for reading. Forms: absolute אֱנוֹשׁ ; construct in Jer 20:10 ( אֱנוֹשׁ שְׁלוֹמִי , "the man of my peace" — my close friend). It is used both of individuals and collectively, and it has no plural of its own in ordinary use — אֲנָשִׁים ( ʾănāšîm , "men") serves the wider root family as the plural of אִישׁ . 2. Root — the incurable root Strong's and BDB both derive enosh from אָנַשׁ ( ʾānaš , H605): "to be weak, sick — incurable." The verb survives in the text almost entirely in one fixed picture: a wound or sickness that cannot be healed. Jer 15:18 — "my wound is incurable ( אֲנוּשָׁה , ʾănûšâ )." Jer 30:12 — "your hurt is incurable ( אָנוּשׁ )." Mic 1:9 — "her wounds are incurable ( אֲנוּשָׁה )." 2 Sam 12:15 uses the verb of David's child: "and he became sick ( וַיֵּאָנַשׁ )." Jer 17:9 — the root lands on the human heart itself: "the heart is deceitful above all things, and incurably sick ( וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא ) — who can know it?" The adjective there is the enosh root, predicated of the heart. See §5. Strong's gloss of the noun follows the root honestly: "properly, a mortal — and thus differing from the more dignified adam." That contrast is Strong's editorial phrasing, but the distribution backs the substance: enosh is the word the poets reach for when the human is being measured against God and found frail. Observation: the derivation from the "incurable" root is the lexica's standard account, stated without BDB's "perhaps." Caution anyway: etymology is not meaning-in-use. Enosh in a given verse means "man/mankind"; the frailty is carried by the contexts (§4) first and the root second. Do not preach the root where the verse is doing something else. 3. Semantic range (BDB) An individual man — Job 5:17 ("happy is the enosh whom God reproves"); Ps 55:14 [Eng. 55:13]; Jer 20:10 (the friend). Men collectively, ordinary men — Isa 24:6; 33:8; Ps 73:5; and the telling idiom of Isa 8:1, חֶרֶט אֱנוֹשׁ — "a common stylus," an ordinary, human-sized pen: enosh as the measure of the commonplace. Man, mankind under the aspect of mortality — the dominant poetic sense: Deut 32:26; Job 7:1, 17; 14:19; 28:13; Isa 51:12. Enosh never names the species in its dignity (that is adam), never marks maleness (that is ish), and is never a word of law or narrative prose if poetry will do. It is the poets' word for us. 4. Biblical examples — Genesis first, then the poetry where it lives Enosh the man — Gen 4:26 (H583, the proper name). "To Seth also a son was born, and he called his name Enosh. Then it was begun to call on the name of YHWH." The third generation from Adam carries the mortal-word as a name — and the calling-on-the-Name begins in his days. docs.b: נֶפֶשׁ — nephesh — Full Hebrew Treatment (Finished, Nov 23, 2026) Labels follow Aaron's rule: observation / interpretation / hypothesis / declaration are kept separate. Read with the ruach study. If one study in this set can change how a person reads the whole Bible, it is this one — because the English word "soul" has been standing in front of nephesh for centuries, saying something nephesh does not say. 1. The word itself Consonantal text: נפש (nun–pe–shin) Pointed text: נֶפֶשׁ Transliteration: nepeš / nephesh — "NEH-fesh" Strong's / lexicon: H5315; TWOT 1395a Part of speech: feminine noun Frequency: BDB's entry is headed 756; other standard counts give 753–754. Quote as "about 755," method named. It is one of the most common nouns in the Bible. Forms: absolute נֶפֶשׁ ; suffixed נַפְשִׁי "my nephesh" (Gen 12:13), נַפְשׁוֹ , נַפְשְׁךָ ; plural נְפָשׁוֹת / נְפָשֹׁת — and the plural is where the word's plainest sense shows: Exod 12:4 counts nephashot per household for the lamb; census texts count nephesh by heads. A nephesh can be counted , because a nephesh is a living person, not a vapour. 2. Root From נָפַשׁ ( nāpaš , H5314), "to breathe, to be refreshed" — used exactly three times as a verb, and the three are load-bearing: Exod 23:12 and 31:17, of rest and refreshment on the seventh day — 31:17 says of God himself, שָׁבַת וַיִּנָּפַשׁ , "he rested and was refreshed" — and 2 Sam 16:14, of David's company refreshing themselves. The noun's background picture: the breathing, and therefore living, and therefore desiring and tiring and reviving, creature. BDB's own summary of the noun's senses runs: "soul, living being, life, self, person, desire, appetite, emotion, and passion" — note that the lexicon's list begins with a being, not a substance. 3. Semantic range (BDB) That which breathes — the living being itself. The inner being as the whole animated self, distinguished from flesh ( בָּשָׂר ) in poetry but never separable from it in the Greek sense (§7). A living being, a creature — of animals first in the text's own order (Gen 1:20, 21, 24, 30) and of the human (Gen 2:7). Life — with the life in the blood. Lev 17:11: "the nephesh of the flesh is in the blood" (see §4). The self, the person — "my nephesh" as a way of saying "I, me": Gen 12:13, "that my nephesh may live because of you" = "that I may live." Pronoun-work, done by a noun. Seat of appetite and desire — the nephesh hungers, thirsts, craves: Deut 12:20, "when your nephesh craves meat"; Ps 42:2 [Eng. 42:1], "my nephesh thirsts for God"; Prov 25:25, good news like cold water "to a weary nephesh." Seat of emotion and passion — the nephesh loves (Song 1:7, "you whom my nephesh loves"), hates (2 Sam 5:8 in a difficult text), grieves (Ps 42–43, "why are you cast down, O my nephesh"), and can be poured out (Ps 42:5 [Eng. 42:4]; Lam 2:12). A dead body, a corpse — the sense English readers never expect: נֶפֶשׁ מֵת , "a dead nephesh" (Num 6:6; Lev 21:11), and nephesh alone for a corpse at Lev 19:28; Num 9:6–10; Hag 2:13. A word that can denote the dead body cannot, without argument, mean "the immortal part that leaves the body." That argument is sometimes made from other texts; it cannot be made from this word. 4. Biblical examples — Genesis first The animals first — Gen 1:20–30. Before any human is called nephesh, the swarming water creatures and the land animals are נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה , "living nephesh" (1:20, 21, 24), and 1:30 gives every beast "nephesh ḥayyah" outright. Whatever nephesh means, the text gives it to the animals four times before it gives it to us. Any definition of nephesh that only fits humans fails the first chapter. The man becomes — Gen 2:7. God breathes nishmat ḥayyim into the formed dust, וַיְהִי הָאָדָם לְנֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה — "and the adam became a living nephesh." The grammar is the doctrine the text actually teaches: the man does not receive a nephesh as a part added to a body; body-plus-breath is a nephesh. docs.b: אוֹר — or — Full Hebrew Treatment (Finished, Nov 23, 2026) Labels follow Aaron's rule: observation / interpretation / hypothesis / declaration are kept separate. This word stands first in the Bible's first act of creation, and it stands inside Aaron's own chosen name — Aharon Ben Or, "Aaron, son of light." Both facts are handled here at the same standard: the text first, the poetry labelled as poetry. 1. The word itself Consonantal text: אור (aleph–vav–resh) Pointed text: אוֹר Transliteration: ʾôr — "OR" Strong's / lexicon: H216; TWOT 52a Part of speech: noun — masculine in most uses; BDB notes it as feminine at Job 36:32 and Jer 13:16. Gender instability in a common noun is a fact of the corpus, printed without embarrassment. Frequency: BDB's entry is headed 121; other counts give 122–123 (KJV translation count 123). Quote as "about 120," method named. Forms: absolute אוֹר ; construct in compounds like אוֹר הַבֹּקֶר , "the light of the morning" (Judg 16:2; 2 Sam 23:4); suffixed אוֹרִי "my light" (Ps 27:1), אוֹרוֹ "his light"; plural אוֹרִים (Ps 136:7), "lights" — on which see §5, the Urim question. The verb: אוֹר (H215), "to be or become light, to shine, to give light" — Gen 1:15's luminaries are appointed לְהָאִיר , "to give light." Noun and verb are one root-family, transparently. 2. Root From the verb אוֹר , "to shine, become light" — one of the least disputed derivations in this series of studies. The noun is the verb's product: light is what shining gives. Where adam, shem, and adamah all carry etymology warnings, or carries almost none; its interest lies in its usage (§3–4) and its traditions (§7), not its pedigree. 3. Semantic range (BDB) Light as diffused in nature — daylight itself (Gen 1:3–5; Job 38:19). Morning light, dawn — אוֹר הַבֹּקֶר , "light of the morning" (Judg 16:2; 1 Sam 14:36; Neh 8:3, reading "from the light [dawn] until midday"); Mic 2:1, men who plot "at the light of morning." Light of the heavenly luminaries — moonlight and sunlight (Isa 30:26), "stars of light" (Ps 148:3). Lightning — Job 36:32; 37:3 (lightning as God's or loosed from his hand). Light of a lamp — the concrete household sense behind the proverbs (§4). Light of life — Job 33:30, "to be enlightened with the light of the living"; Ps 56:14 [Eng. 56:13], walking "in the light of life." Light of prosperity — light as wellbeing: Esth 8:16, "the Jews had light and gladness"; Job 22:28, "light will shine on your ways"; Isa 58:8, 10, the fast God chooses makes "your light break forth like dawn" and rise "in the darkness." Light of instruction — Prov 6:23: "the commandment is a lamp ( נֵר ) and the teaching (Torah) is light ( אוֹר )"; Ps 119:105: "your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path." Light of the face — the shining face as favour: "the light of the king's face is life" (Prov 16:15); "lift up the light of your face upon us" (Ps 4:7 [Eng. 4:6]; Num 6:25, "make his face shine upon you" — the verb form). YHWH as light — Ps 27:1: "YHWH is my light ( אוֹרִי ) and my salvation"; Mic 7:8: "when I sit in darkness, YHWH is a light to me"; Isa 60:19–20, the eschatological form: "the sun shall no longer be your light by day... but YHWH shall be your everlasting light." The range runs one way: from physics to favour. Daylight is the picture; everything else — prosperity, teaching, God's face, God himself — is the picture extended, and the extensions never cut loose from the picture. That is how Hebrew metaphor works, and or is its cleanest exhibit. 4. Biblical examples — Genesis 1 first, where the word is born The first word spoken over the world — Gen 1:3–5. וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים יְהִי אוֹר וַיְהִי־אוֹר — "And God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light." Or is the first created thing named in the Bible, and it is created by speech — the shem study's world, where words carry acts, begins here. docs.b: רוּחַ — ruach — Full Hebrew Treatment (Finished, Nov 23, 2026) Labels follow Aaron's rule: observation / interpretation / hypothesis / declaration are kept separate. Read with the nephesh study: רוּחַ and נֶפֶשׁ are the two breath-words, and the text keeps them distinguishable even where English flattens both into "spirit/soul." 1. The word itself Consonantal text: רוח (resh–vav–ḥet) Pointed text: רוּחַ Transliteration: rûaḥ — "ROO-akh" (final ḥet sounded in the throat) Strong's / lexicon: H7307; TWOT 2131a Part of speech: noun, usually feminine, occasionally masculine (BDB notes the masculine use at Exod 10:13 and elsewhere) — one of the few Hebrew nouns that swings gender, which the versions mostly hide. Frequency: 378 occurrences (BDB head-count; the standard figure quoted across the lexica). BDB's entry helpfully counts its own senses — breath 33×, wind 117×, temper/disposition-spirit 76×, the spirit of the living being 25×, the spirit of God 94× — and those sub-counts are used in §3 with their source named. Forms: absolute רוּחַ ; construct identical ( רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים , "ruach of God"); suffixed רוּחִי "my ruach" (Gen 6:3), רוּחֲךָ "your ruach" (Ps 104:30); plural רוּחוֹת , "winds/spirits" (Ps 104:4; Num 16:22, "God of the ruchot of all flesh"). 2. Root Strong's: from רוּחַ the verb (H7306), "to breathe, blow" — the noun is moving air, wherever it moves: in the sky, in the chest, in the temper, from God. The lexica treat the connection as straightforward; unlike adam and shem, this word's root is not a fight. A neighbouring derivative matters for §5: רֵיחַ ( rêaḥ , "smell, scent," H7381) is listed by the lexica from the same breathing/blowing stock — air carrying something to the nose. Print as lexicon arrangement, not as a sermon. 3. Semantic range (BDB, with BDB's own counts) Breath of mouth or nostrils (33×) — Job's "my breath is strange to my wife" (19:17); and thinned to nothing: "windy words" (Job 16:3), prophets who "shall become ruach" — mere air (Jer 5:13). Wind (117×) — the east wind that brings the locusts and the sea-wind that takes them (Exod 10:13, 19); the wind God sends over the flood waters (Gen 8:1); the four winds as the quarters of the sky (Jer 49:36) — hence ruach can even mean a side/direction . Spirit as temper, disposition, animation (76×) — that which breathes fast when a person is stirred: Pharaoh's ruach troubled (Gen 41:8); "shortness of ruach" for impatience (Exod 6:9); a haughty ruach before a fall (Prov 16:18); the ruach that revives when Jacob hears Joseph lives (Gen 45:27). The spirit of the living being in flesh, men and animals (25×) — Gen 6:17; 7:15, "all flesh in which is ruach ḥayyim, the breath/spirit of life"; Eccl 3:21 asks who knows whether the ruach of man goes upward and the ruach of the beast down — a question the text leaves open, and this study leaves it where the text did. The spirit of God (94×) — creating, equipping, prophesying, judging: §4. BDB notes the phrase is absent from Deuteronomy and Jeremiah — a distribution fact worth knowing before anyone builds a doctrine on the phrase's frequency. The centre: ruach is air in motion with effects . Every sense — weather, breath, mood, God's action — is that one picture at a different scale. English needs three words (wind/breath/spirit) for what Hebrew does with one, and every translation choice in §8 is a loss managed, not a problem solved. 4. Biblical examples — Genesis first Over the waters — Gen 1:2. וְרוּחַ אֱלֹהִים מְרַחֶפֶת עַל־פְּנֵי הַמָּיִם — "and ruach elohim was hovering over the face of the waters." The Bible's second verse, and its most argued ruach: "the Spirit of God" (traditional), "a wind from God" (NRSV), "a wind from God sweeping" (NJPS), Speiser's "an awesome wind." The participle מְרַחֶפֶת ( məraḥepet , hovering/fluttering) is used again of the eagle over its nest in Deut 32:11 — the text's own second use of a rare word, and the strongest internal clue to the picture. docs.b: שֵׁם — shem — Full Hebrew Treatment (Finished, Nov 23, 2026) Labels follow Aaron's rule: observation / interpretation / hypothesis / declaration are kept separate. Completion note (Nov 23, 2026): reviewed against the full-treatment standard — spelling (consonantal + pointed), transliteration, root, morphology, semantic range, biblical examples, ancient context, wordplay, cognates, translation alternatives, traditions, uncertainties. Two sections were missing and are now added: §4b (wordplay) and §6b (ancient Near Eastern context). Everything else stood as drafted. 1. The word itself Consonantal text: שׁם (shin–mem) Pointed text: שֵׁם Transliteration: shem (pronounced approx. "shame" in Strong's phonetic guide) Strong's / lexicon: H8034; TWOT 2405 Part of speech: masculine noun Plural: שֵׁמוֹת ( shemot , "names") Construct / suffixed forms: שֵׁם־ (construct, "name of"), שְׁמִי ("my name"), שִׁמְךָ ("your name"), שְׁמוֹ ("his name"), בְּשֵׁם ("in the name of") Frequency (lexicon counts, method matters): BibleTools/Strong's counts 865 uses in the KJV text; Blue Letter Bible counts the form in 771 verses (NASB95 concordance). The two numbers count different things (occurrences vs. verses), so do not quote either without its method. 2. Root — uncertain, and that matters Brown-Driver-Briggs calls shem a "primitive word," perhaps derived from שׂוּם ( śûm , H7760, "to put, place, set") through the idea of a "definite and conspicuous position" — i.e. a name as something set up, made conspicuous, a mark of individuality. Observation: the lexicon entry hedges with "perhaps." Interpretation: the "set up / made conspicuous" reading fits the memorial/monument sense below, but it is not a proven etymology. Do not upgrade: do not present śûm → shem as established fact. 3. Semantic range (BDB) Name — a person's, place's, or thing's designation. Reputation, fame, glory — what the name carries. The Name (as designation of God) — ha-Shem , "the Name," used especially where the divine name itself is not pronounced. Memorial, monument — a name as something left standing after a person. Strong's adds the implications: honour, authority, character. In short: in Hebrew thought a name is not only a label. It is identity, standing, reputation, and presence — the person as known. 4. Biblical examples, by sense Plain naming — Genesis is full of it. Gen 2:11 — "The name of the first [river] is Pishon." Naming marks and orders the world as Adam encounters it. Gen 4:26 and Gen 12:8 / 13:4 — people begin to "call on the name of YHWH." Calling on the name is not reciting a label; it is invoking the one named. Making a name — reputation as a project. Gen 11:4 (Babel) — "let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered." The tower story turns on shem : a self-made name, set up against scattering. Read against Gen 12:2, where Abram is told "I will make your name great" — a name given , not seized. The contrast is the point, and it is in the text, not imposed on it. Gen 5:32; 10 — Shem, son of Noah, bears the same spelling, שֵׁם . Whether the personal name means "name/renown" is plausible but not stated in the text; the text does not gloss it. Do not claim it as the text's own etymology. The Name of God — presence, not a password. Exod 3:13–15 — Moses asks, "What is his name?" The answer is not a dictionary entry but a self-declaration: "I AM WHO I AM" / YHWH. The name discloses character and presence, and it is given in a commissioning ("say this to the Israelites"), not as private information. Exod 20:7 — "You shall not take up the name of YHWH your God in vain [for emptiness/falsehood]." The prohibition is about carrying the name lightly or falsely, not only about pronouncing syllables. Deut 12:5, 11 — God will choose "a place to put his name there." The name dwells: presence is located, not abstract. Deut 18:19–22; Jer 14:14 — prophets speak "in my name" or falsely in it. Speaking in a name claims the authority of the one named — which is why false use i

docs.h: The Sending Test — Remnant Lab · Scroll of Fire A blind sending test that honestly tests telepathy and foresight claims: the target list is sealed with a fingerprint before the first guess, scored against chance, and kept only on your device. How the test stays honest Run a session The targets are locked in What the numbers say Your sessions on this device What would count as evidence Luck runs in streaks What others tried
docs.b: Remnant Lab · Test an Instrument The Sending Test Experimental People talk about telepathy — one mind reaching another — and about foresight, knowing something before it happens. Talk is cheap either way. This tool does not ask you to believe or to disbelieve. It lets you run the test cleanly : a fixed number of tries, targets sealed before the first guess, and a score measured honestly against chance. The protocol — read this first How the test stays honest You fix the length first. A session is 20 or 40 tries, chosen before anything is drawn. You cannot quietly stop early on a lucky streak or stretch a session until it looks good.

The targets are sealed. When the session starts, the page draws the whole list of targets from a secret seed — a starting number the draw grows from — and locks it in a box. The box's fingerprint is shown to you before the first guess: a long code made from the list (a SHA-256 hash). If the list were changed afterward, the fingerprint would no longer match, and at the end you can check it yourself. Chance is one in four. Each try offers four symbols and exactly one is the target. Guessing blindly scores about 5 hits in 20 tries, or 10 in 40 — and luck alone sometimes runs higher. The scoring below says exactly how often. Everything is revealed at the end. The seed and the full target list are shown, the seal is re-checked in front of you, and the session is kept on this device only. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Run a session Choose how to test Receiver — tests telepathy, mind to mind. Two people, one phone. A sender is shown each target and holds it in mind; the receiver, who never saw it, picks. Foresight — tests precognition, knowing before. One person. You pick first — but understand what that means here: the whole target list was already drawn and sealed before you started. Nothing is drawn after you guess. You are testing whether your picks line up with a list that was already fixed, which is exactly the claim foresight makes. Choose the length — fixed once you start 20 tries — chance averages 5 hits; luck alone reaches 9 or more about 1 time in 25. 40 tries — chance averages 10 hits; luck alone reaches 16 or more about 1 time in 38. Draw and seal the targets Sealed

The targets are locked in Fingerprint: The full fingerprint (the commitment) Write it down if you like. After the session, the list and the seed are revealed, and this page re-makes the fingerprint from them in front of you. If even one target had been changed after your guesses, the fingerprints would not match. Begin trial 1 Sender — this screen is for your eyes only Look at this symbol. Hold it in mind — its shape, its feel. When you are holding it, tap the button and hand the phone to the receiver. The target will not be shown again until the receiver has picked. ● Send the Circle I am holding it in mind — hide it and pass the phone ● Circle ▲ Triangle ≋ Waves ★ Star Next trial Result

What the numbers say The reveal — check the seal yourself The seed this session was drawn from: The full target list, in order: The fingerprint shown before the first guess: Re-check the seal now This session was saved to this device only — see your sessions below. Nothing was uploaded anywhere. Run another session Your sessions on this device Sessions live in this browser, on this device, and nowhere else. One strong session means little; a record that repeats is what would count — so the record is kept whole, seals and all, and you can take a copy with you. No sessions yet. Run one above and it will be kept here.

Download a backup of my sessions The backup is one file holding every session whole — targets, guesses, and fingerprints — so the record can be re-checked anywhere, the same way the Life Atlas backup door works. The file contains your session record; keep it where you keep your own things. Reading a result What would count as evidence Three things, all built into this tool: targets sealed before the first guess, a trial count fixed in advance, and a record anyone can re-check. A claim tested any other way — targets chosen after, sessions stopped when they look good, records nobody can verify — has not really been tested at all.

And the hard part: even a score outside the luck line, once, is not proof. Luck deals somebody an unlikely session every day. What would count is the same result, outside the line, repeating across many sealed sessions. Why small samples mislead Luck runs in streaks In 20 tries, luck alone reaches 8 hits about 1 time in 10 — that feels like something, and it is nothing but luck doing what luck does. It reaches 9 or more about 1 time in 25. Short runs swing wildly; that is why this tool fixes the count up front and why its verdict always names how often luck alone would do at least as well. History — labeled as history

What others tried In the 1970s through the 1990s, researchers ran "Ganzfeld" sessions: a receiver resting in soft, even light and sound, a sender viewing a picture or a clip, then the receiver picking it from four choices — the same one-in-four shape as this tool. Some combined reports put the hit rate above chance; other researchers argued the methods leaked or the counting was generous. Decades later it is still argued, both ways. The lesson that survives the argument is the protocol: seal the targets, fix the count, keep the record — which is what this page does. docs.b: Shipping, Timing & Returns Plain words, the way this shop actually works — read them before you write, and keep your confirmation email: it is your order's whole record. Timing Every piece is made to order or finished by hand after your order is confirmed. Your timing is given in writing in that confirmation, before you pay — if the forge cannot meet it, you hear so before any money moves, never after. Photographed before it ships Before a piece leaves, it is photographed and entered in the registry under its code. The registry record — origin, material, handwork, release — is your piece's provenance, and it stays standing on this page. Shipping Pieces ship as tracked parcels to addresses in the United States, and the shipping cost is named in your written confirmation — never a surprise added at the door. Outside the United States: ask first by email, and it is confirmed case by case before any payment. If something is wrong If a piece arrives damaged, or does not match what was confirmed — sizing, finish, orientation — write promptly on delivery, with a photo if it helps. Aaron will repair it, reforge it, or refund it: the maker's word is the warranty, and it is kept. Returns Made-to-order work is made for one person's wrist and measure, so change-of-mind returns are not taken on custom pieces. The confirmation step exists for exactly this reason: the piece is right on paper before it exists in copper. Nothing here limits any right your own law gives you.

Copper, honestly Natural copper darkens and takes a patina as it is worn — that is the metal being itself, and the sealed finish slows it. Copper can leave a green mark on skin for some wearers; it washes off and harms nothing. If that would bother you, choose the sealed finish at confirmation. docs.b: Symbolic meaning Names such as calm, focus, restore, dream, remnant, crown, or lift. These describe the intended frame, not guaranteed biological effects. The Frequency system is a creative and observational tool. Symbolic presets should not be presented as medical treatment, diagnosis, or proof that one named number produces a universal outcome. Equation 17 · Voice Carriers The Carrier Form $$ \boxed{ \mathbf{V}(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k \cos\left( 2\pi\nu_k t+\phi_k \right) } $$ A carrier field \( \mathbf{V}(t) \) can be modeled as multiple components, each with amplitude \(a_k\), frequency \( \nu_k \), and phase \( \phi_k \). ν

Frequency The number of cycles per second, measured in hertz. a Amplitude The signal level. Perceived loudness also depends on frequency, equipment, room, and listener. φ Phase The relative position of a waveform inside its cycle. t Duration The time through which the carrier is active and changing. Measured Relations The physical layer of the console. Single tone $$ y(t)=A\sin(2\pi f t+\phi) $$ A basic oscillator defined by amplitude, frequency, time, and phase. Beat relation $$ f_{\mathrm{beat}} = \left|f_1-f_2\right| $$ Two nearby tones can create a slower amplitude pattern equal to their frequency difference.

Phase difference $$ \Delta\phi=\phi_2-\phi_1 $$ Relative phase affects reinforcement, cancellation, motion, and stereo perception. Mixed field $$ x_{\mathrm{mix}}(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{n}g_kx_k(t) $$ Each deck or source enters the master field through its own gain \(g_k\). Equation 3 The Harmonic Gate decides what enters. $$ \boxed{ \mathcal{H}(\nu)\in[0,1] } $$ The gate may reject a carrier, reduce it, or allow it to pass fully. In the console this can correspond to mute, gain, filter, solo, crossfade, routing, or a declared session rule. Technical gate Volume limit, frequency range, filter, channel, duration, fade, and output device.

Intent gate The stated purpose of the session and which sounds support or conflict with it. Witness gate What can be recorded as observation and what must remain interpretation. Ethical gate Consent, safe level, transparent playback, and immediate stop conditions. Open Equation 3 Equation 6 The Type-7 field combines governed carriers. $$ \boxed{ \mathbb{T}_{7}(t) = \bigoplus_{\nu\in\Gamma} \operatorname{PL} \left[ \mathbf{V}(\nu) \right] } $$ The Type-7 form represents multiple selected carriers coordinated through declared phase, timing, gain, and intention. Here, phase-locking is a design operation inside the sound system, not proof of an unseen physical field beyond the measured output.

3 Carrier selection Choose tones, pulses, rhythm, timbre, and voice according to the declared frame. 4 Harmonic gate Set gain, filters, routing, duration, mute, solo, and stop conditions. 5 Field playback Run the session with visible controls and a known master level. 6 Witness Record measured settings and reported experience separately. 7 Coherence review Compare the intended field with the actual sound, listener response, and technical output. 8 Remnant Save only the settings, interpretations, and conclusions that survive review. Calm Lower intensity, gradual movement, reduced rhythmic density, and a clearly limited duration. Focus Stable carrier relationships, minimal distraction, defined task window, and consistent level. Clarity Sparser layering, stronger separation between carriers, and emphasis on intelligibility. Restore A gentle transition field framed around rest, breathing, or returning after strain. Create A more dynamic field designed to support movement, making, writing, drawing, or building. Dream A low-demand symbolic field with slow transitions and explicit volume limits. docs.b: An artifact moves through states. 01 Concept The idea, sketch, material search, and initial symbolic frame. 02 In Creation Construction has begun, but the form and registry entry remain open. 03 Completed The physical build is stable enough for inspection, photography, and classification. 04 Registered The artifact receives its code, name, materials, status, and public record. 05 Active The artifact is worn, used, tested, displayed, gifted, offered, or held as a personal instrument. 06 Maintained Cleaning, repair, resizing, rewinding, replacement, or condition updates preserve continuity. 07 Transferred Stewardship changes through gift, sale, inheritance, return, or reassignment. 08 Archived or Retired The artifact leaves active use but remains part of the historical registry. Stewardship

Ownership does not erase relationship. Care Store, clean, wear, transport, and display the artifact according to its actual materials and construction. Continuity Preserve the code, name, maker, core materials, and known history when transferring or modifying the object. Correction Notify the registry when an important material, condition, status, or performance description is found to be wrong. Respect Symbolic meaning can be changed by a keeper, but the original maker’s declared meaning should not be silently rewritten as though it never existed. Repair Record visible repairs and replacement materials when they alter the object’s form, function, value, or history.

Release A steward may gift, sell, return, archive, or retire an artifact according to the terms and responsibilities attached to it. Ethical Registry Mythic presentation must not become deceptive representation. Accurate materials Do not misidentify stone, metal, glass, coating, magnet type, reclaimed source, or construction. Accurate status Available, Reserved, Gifted, Personal, and Sold should match the object’s actual status. Accurate images Promotional backgrounds may be stylized, but the artifact itself should remain recognizable and not materially altered without disclosure. Accurate claims Separate symbolism, intention, personal witness, and testable performance.

Transparent price When offered, the price, availability method, shipping or transfer terms, and major condition issues should be clear. Status is time-dependent Available, Reserved, Gifted, Personal Instrument, In Creation, Coming Soon, Archived, Retired, and Not for Sale are not permanent identities. The registry should record when status changes and why. Registry Layers Seven layers make an artifact legible. M Material Copper, stone, glass, ferrite, magnets, fiber, leather, wood, adhesive, reclaimed source, dimensions, condition, and material limits. D Design Geometry, weave, winding, structure, fastening, stone placement, interfaces, version, and intended function. N Name Title, translation, code, class, subtitle, story, symbolic language, and position inside the Codex.

P Provenance Maker, date, location, source materials, ownership, gifting, sale, transfer, and chain of stewardship. W Witness Build photographs, field notes, measurements, direct observation, keeper reports, condition checks, and documented revision. Mτ Memory The accumulated story of making, use, travel, repair, transfer, interpretation, and later remembrance. St Status Current availability, ownership, release stage, condition, registry visibility, and permitted transfer. Classification Artifact classes describe relationship and use. Personal Instrument Built for the maker or a designated operator.

Usually retained, tested, and developed as part of the active Living Technology system. Wearable Artifact A ring, band, pendant, wrist node, or other piece designed to be carried on the body. Gifted Artifact Transferred without sale as a deliberate relationship between maker, object, and keeper. Registry Release An artifact made available for purchase or inquiry with visible materials, status, price, and transfer terms. Archive Piece Retained as a completed historical object, reference build, earlier version, or non-released record. Unreleased / In Creation A work whose final structure, name, status, price, or claim language has not yet been completed.

Naming A name should deepen the object without hiding what it is. 1 Registry code A stable identifier such as T7-000, HL-001, TN-001, or TS-001. 2 Primary name The recognized title used across the registry, images, posts, and documentation. 3 Translation or subtitle A second language, descriptive phrase, or mythic title that adds context. 4 Class The practical relationship: Personal Instrument, Gifted Artifact, Wearable Artifact, Archive Piece, or Registry Release. 5 Material description A direct account of what the object is physically made from. 6 Mythic description The symbolic story, archetype, memory, or meaning carried by the name.

Maker record Who built the artifact, when, where, under what project, and through which version or revision. Transfer record Gift, sale, reservation, inheritance, return, or keeper change should be dated when the parties choose to preserve that history. docs.b: Provenance should not expose private personal information unnecessarily. The registry can preserve continuity while limiting names, addresses, transaction details, or other identifying data. Claim Layers What an artifact means is not always what it proves. Material Verified composition The metals, stones, glass, fibers, magnets, cores, fasteners, coatings, and visible construction. Design Declared function What the maker intended the structure, geometry, arrangement, or wearable form to do. Witness Observed experience What a maker or keeper directly noticed, measured, felt, or recorded under stated conditions.

Interpretation Proposed meaning The theory connecting the artifact to a field, pattern, memory, carrier, place, or operator experience. Symbolism Mythic and personal language The story, title, archetype, spiritual meaning, cultural reference, or private relationship carried by the artifact. Performance Repeatable effect A claim that the artifact reliably causes a defined outcome. This requires the strongest evidence and the narrowest wording. Registration Protocol From finished object to living record. Register what exists—not what the object may someday become. Future plans, symbolic possibilities, and testable hypotheses can be included, but the current build, status, condition, and claim level should remain clear.
